why: Apart mostly for what is missing: its retrieval exists only as test stand-ins, so it has no search, and key-value plus graph storage is an uncommon pair. Unfinished more than unusual.

A real design outlier: each claim carries a nine-value certainty status that only an operator can promote, in key-value and graph stores with no search. Pre-alpha, so mostly design rather than proven use.
The 2023 research original. It predates what later systems settled on (keyword search, a database, per-user scoping, committed tests), so it sits apart as the ancestor, not as a new idea.
A retrieval research method more than a product: it hands storage to vector databases and lets a graph algorithm decide what to recall. Few systems delegate storage and route recall that way.
Deliberately skips search: it keeps structured memories in SQLite and loads the recent window for the model to read, with a background merger. Rejecting retrieval outright is what separates it.
Half of a system: the injection side of a loop with a built-in no-memory control group, its storage elsewhere and its hooks never registered. The partial, experimental shape keeps it apart.
A shared store of errors, the fixes tried and whether they worked, across four coding tools. Recording outcomes rather than facts is uncommon, and it has no search or scoping.
The MemGPT-lineage server, where the agent edits its own memory blocks. Storage is delegated and its source now sits on an archive branch: an early, influential design the corpus moved away from.
Not a memory system: a coding harness with session branches and compaction but no memory model. Nearly every field reads none, which puts it far from everything that has a store.
A verification design: a confident claim needs a quote checked word for word against its source, and a failed check is recorded. Strong on trust and review with no search, which few systems pair.
Rare and well built: forgetting by archiving to cold storage, a block on rejected values returning, and human review. Few systems combine all three, here on Chroma with hooks into Claude Code.
A browser agent whose learned site maps wait in staging until a person switches them on. Human approval of agent-written memory is rare, and it lives in a browser panel rather than a database.
A recipe more than a system: hooks and a nightly importer file sessions into an Obsidian vault for a person to read. A hand-curated vault with no search sits apart from engineered stores.
Turns your documents into training data for a personal model. Memory that ends up in model weights is unusual, and deleting from its vector store does not remove what the model learned.
A research pipeline whose memory mostly lives and dies inside one run; its one lasting memory is a skill file. Memory meant to persist that mostly does not makes the profile odd.
Extracted memories wait as pending until a person approves, rejects or edits each one: the most literal human-in-the-loop design here, on a graph store, which few systems match.

A service splitting short-lived working memory from extracted long-term memory, with pluggable extraction. Ordinary ideas, but Redis plus delegated storage plus model-assisted recall is an uncommon mix.
Proposes new skills and waits for approval, then forgets every rejection when the process exits. Approval-gated skill memory is rare; losing the rejections is the weak spot.
A dormant 2024 library with a complete add, replace, delete and get interface but in-memory storage and no scoping. An older, simpler shape that 2026 systems no longer resemble.
Its memory is about the agent itself: a versioned risk profile built from the agent's own audit history and read before each decision. A unique subject for memory, with human review and no search.
A storage engine with a token-budgeted context pack whose world-time field and scope rule exist but are barely wired. Key-value storage plus model extraction plus unused features make an odd profile.
A wiki compiled from documents with no embeddings: the agent walks an index of pages and the model decides where knowledge goes. Choosing a browsable wiki over vector search sets it apart.
Built around refusing expensive work: a gate decides whether to retrieve at all, and merging is batched. Delegated storage and hard deletes with no scoping make a lean, uncommon shape.

Memory inside a coding agent, off by default: a model extracts past sessions into SQLite and a locked-down sub-agent rewrites a Markdown folder from a git diff, so forgetting is a diff it must act on. A database and files, consolidation, pruning and age-out together are a combination few others use.
A thinking layer over a shared knowledge-graph protocol, with budgeted recall and memories that expire. Graph recall over delegated storage, with a status field, is a combination few others use.

File-based context whose background merging is fenced to one folder, tested against a corpus built from a paper on memory corruption. Strong on review and provenance with no search: a verification outlier.
An adapter layer whose local and remote backends must rank results identically, with a model in the recall path. It sits apart for being an adapter over other stores rather than a store.

A large Rust server mixing key-value storage, graph recall, summarising and merging. Its committed self-audit is the notable part; the position comes from that uncommon mix of storage and background work.
Memory inside an LLM traffic router rather than an agent: typed memories, vector stores and an injection gate in one process. Where it lives, more than how it remembers, sets it apart.
An agent works in a typed graph of episodes, hypotheses and tasks, and can read any node as it stood at a past moment. Graph plus key-value storage with time travel is a rare pairing.
Distinguished more by its history than its mechanics: the schema records why seven unused fields were removed. Decay and a status field without a database or search arm make an unusual profile.

A coding agent with three memory tiers, one committed to the repository, that refuses to store secrets unconditionally. Human review and background reprocessing without search are uncommon among coding agents.
A 423-line experiment that stores every fact in one fixed-size holographic vector and never forgets. A mathematical representation of memory unlike any database-backed design here.
A skill book whose de-duplicator remembers which pairs it decided not to merge, and checks that before proposing again. Remembering a decision not to merge is rare.
A simulation engine whose only channel to a language model is a validated projection; its memory store is barely used. Apart for being a simulator with memory attached rather than a memory system.
An addressed mailbox inside memory: one session leaves a note that the next session delivers and marks read. Messages between sessions, with expiry and enforced provenance, are a rare use of memory.

A brain-inspired wrapper over a graph memory, adding a forgetting curve and point-in-time search. Graph storage with background passes and partitioning is uncommon; its time filter is only weakly tested.
Indexes the transcripts agents already wrote to disk instead of recording from scratch, removing secrets as it goes. Building memory from files that already exist is the difference.
A research system where model-written notes link to and rewrite neighbouring memories. Notes that change each other sit apart from designs that only append or overwrite.
Its standout is a crash-test harness that kills the process mid-write and checks recovery exactly. That rigour plus tracking when facts were valid puts it among rare, well-built systems.

Grades every record on confidence, importance and durability, keeps a subconscious tier and lets the user pause learning. Heavy background work (pruning, summarising, merging) without vector search is the unusual mix.
Memory inside a trading system: a Neo4j graph fed by indexers, with an agent filter applied only when a caller asks. Graph-first memory in a domain application, not an agent tool, is the difference.
Object memory for robots, built from camera input, saved as one file and queried by spatial relations. Physical-world memory, far from the text-based agent stores around it.
A tamper-evident local ledger for coding agents, hash-chained and verified in both directions, with approvals tied to what they approve. An audit-first design over plain files.

A plugin that syncs each coding agent's own session folders through a private repository, beside a store of content-hashed notes whose forget markers sync ahead of them. Plain session sync paired with a store built so a forgotten note stays forgotten is an unusual shape.
A provider interface rather than a store: every call carries an owner key, with retry and metrics added around any backend. It sits apart as a contract for other memories, not a memory.
An agent runtime whose memory is entirely expiring cache behind an access gate. Memory that is only a cache is unusual when most systems here keep things for good.
A knowledge graph plus two JSON files, ranked only by how often an entity is mentioned, and sorted the wrong way. Apart more for its simplicity than for its ideas.
A merging protocol that is required to remove entries and checks that each deletion happened. Designing for deliberate forgetting is rare when most systems only add.

An institutional record in version control where every thought has a lifecycle status and recall returns only approved, current records. Approval and status without a database or vector search: rare and well built.
